acquisitions.question: Has anyone other than you — a partner, a grandparent, or a daycare staff member — independently described a pickup as difficult?

hypotheses_retained: Pickup difficulty is tied to the transition itself, being collected and leaving, rather than to the daycare day: distress peaks at the door and eases once the child is in the car.
Pickup distress reflects a cumulative end-of-day load (fatigue, hunger, or overstimulation) that peaks at the end of the daycare day, so any collection at that hour would be hard.

The apparent consistency of the pickup pattern is partly a single-source reporting artifact: one caregiver supplies every account, so it may reflect that observer's attention, threshold, or own end-of-day state as much as the child's behaviour.

acquisitions.question: On the three distressed pickup days, was the child collected at the later end of the 15:00-17:30 window (after about 16:30)?

hypotheses_retained: Handover/separation-specific pickup distress: triggered by the handover at the door with the parent and easing once the child is away from the setting. Re-evaluation: remains a live rival, but 'calmer in the car' is non-discriminating (leaving the setting and shedding end-of-day load coincide), and time-invariance within the verified 15:00-17:30 window is untested because no report records pickup time and all support is single-observer.

End-of-day accumulation (fatigue, hunger, overstimulation) in the late-afternoon window, worsening the later within the verified 15:00-17:30 collection window and easing once the child leaves and refuels (last snack 14:30). Re-evaluation: no report records pickup time, so worsening-with-lateness is untested, and 'calmer in the car' fits load removal as well as ending the separation.

Successor to the setting/handover-event account: distress tied to a specific daycare-environment or handover element on those particular days (a person, an activity ending, an item) rather than a general separation or fatigue pattern. Re-evaluation: still undiscriminated by current evidence; three consecutive uniform reports weakly disfavour a rare day-specific trigger, but the sample is small and single-observer.
The difficulty is transition-specific: the child reacts to the handover moment from daycare staff to parent (reunion/transition distress), and the distress resolves once the handover is over.

The difficulty is end-of-day depletion: accumulated fatigue, hunger, or sensory load leaves the child without reserves at the end of the daycare day, independent of who collects them or how the handover goes.

The difficulty is setting-specific: something distressing happens at daycare (a conflict, a change in routine, an uncomfortable incident) that the parent is not told about, so the child discharges the upset at the first safe contact.

The distress is a transition/reunion reaction specific to pickup: the change of setting and re-encounter with the parent is itself dysregulating, and the child settles once the transition is complete.

The distress reflects cumulative end-of-day dysregulation (fatigue, hunger or sensory load) rather than the pickup transition itself; settling in the car may simply mark removal from the taxing setting.
A specific person, place or recurring event within the daycare setting is the trigger, with distress surfacing around the end-of-day period rather than being caused by the reunion itself.
